stem:
Consider this statement about one meeting:
"The meeting is on Monday or the meeting is in Room 2."

In which situation is the statement false?
choices: The meeting is on Monday in Room 5.
The meeting is on Friday in Room 2.
The meeting is on Monday in Room 2.
The meeting is on Friday in Room 5.
answer: The meeting is on Friday in Room 5.
hints: An "or" statement is false in only one kind of situation. Find it.
For every choice, mark each part: is the meeting on Monday? Is it in Room 2?
"Or" is true when at least one part is true, including when both are true. It is false only when both parts are false. Find the choice where neither part holds.

solution.methodName: Mark each part true or false, then combine

steps.action: Split the statement: part 1 is "on Monday"; part 2 is "in Room 2".
An "or" statement is false only when both parts are false.
steps.why: In logic, "or" means "at least one". It is still true when both parts are true.

steps.action: Monday in Room 5: part 1 is true, so the statement is true.
Friday in Room 2: part 2 is true, so the statement is true.
Monday in Room 2: both parts are true, so the statement is true.
steps.why: Logic's "or" is inclusive: both parts being true does not make it false.

steps.action: Friday in Room 5: part 1 is false and part 2 is false, so the statement is false.
The answer is "The meeting is on Friday in Room 5."

The meeting is on Monday, so part 1 is true. One true part makes an "or" statement true.
The meeting is in Room 2, so part 2 is true. One true part makes an "or" statement true.
Many people read "or" as "one but not both". In logic, "or" is still true when both parts are true. Here both parts are true, so the statement is true.
